Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset S^3$ be a compact smooth three-manifold with smooth boundary and let a finite disjoint family of smooth rank-two embedded disks be proper in the following broad sense: each disk has its boundary in $\partial U$ and its interior in $\operatorname{Int}U$. No transversality at its boundary is required. Suppose the topological cut components are three-balls. Then the disks can be replaced by arbitrarily $C^1$-close neat compression disks with exactly the SAME boundary curves, unchanged outside arbitrarily small boundary collars. The new topological cut components correspond to the old ones. After ordinary finite smooth corner rounding the new components are smoothly parametrized standard balls, with labelled disk faces and compatible product collars. Reattaching the disk neighborhoods recovers the actual $U$ and the new disks as their cocores.

The replacement can be supported away from any fixed compact set disjoint from the disk boundary collars, in particular the actual knot arcs and any supplied simultaneous bridge witnesses disjoint from the disks. These objects, their endpoints, ordered pairing and face avoidance are retained. Only the auxiliary compression witnesses change; the surface, attaching curves and actual knot stay fixed. The transport across the initial tangency is a boundary-fixing homeomorphism, smooth separately off its tangency edges; a smooth ambient boundary-preserving diffeomorphism changing tangency is not claimed. The smooth standard-ball assertion uses the full smooth three-dimensional Schoenflies theorem under Countable Choice, rather than a general topological smoothing theorem.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

For $T^2=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$ pointed at $([0],[0])$,

$$\pi_1(T^2,([0],[0]))\cong(\mathbb Z,+)\times(\mathbb Z,+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix an actual balanced multipointed diagram of one oriented knot in $S^3$, of genus $h$, with $k$ ordered pairs of marks and $m=h+k-1>0$, with the smooth pointed-data convention. Fix its surface complex structure, product-integrable generator charts and nearly symmetric tame target data. For any two REALIZED continuous Whitney classes $u,v$ with the same ordered generators, let $D(u),D(v)$ be their integral region domains and let $\mu(u),\mu(v)$ be their actual fixed-end real indices before translation, defined using smooth fixed-end representatives. Then
$$\mu(u)-\mu(v)=2\sum_{i=1}^k(n_{w_i}(u)-n_{w_i}(v))=2\sum_{i=1}^k(n_{z_i}(u)-n_{z_i}(v)).$$
All signed marked degrees are allowed. Thus $\mu-2\sum n_w$ and $\sum n_z-\sum n_w$ depend only on the ordered endpoints among realized classes. In particular every actual same-generator class has $\mu=2\sum n_w=2\sum n_z$. No clean incidence presentation, disjointness of the two endpoint coordinate sets, holomorphic representative, or vanishing marked multiplicity is assumed.

This is an endpoint-difference formula. It does not identify the general region Euler/corner expression, choose an absolute grading normalization, prove that every generator pair admits a Whitney class, or establish analytic counts, cancellation, invariance or comparison. If $m=0$, the point target has only constant maps and the same equalities read zero equals zero.

Assume countable choice. Retain the compact target, totally real boundary submanifolds, fixed path $J_t$ and exact product generator charts of the smooth relative-homotopy index lemma. A continuous Whitney representative from $x$ to $y$ is a continuous disk map with two specified boundary points mapped to $x,y$ and its two boundary arcs mapped into $L_0,L_1$. Equivalence means an actual continuous relative homotopy fixing those points and preserving the two boundary conditions.

Every such class has a smooth fixed-end strip representative, constant on full tails. If two smooth fixed-end representatives are continuously relatively homotopic, there is a smooth relative homotopy between them with one common pair of constant tails and the same fixed endpoints. Consequently the quotient of smooth fixed-end representatives by those smooth homotopies identifies with the continuous Whitney-class set. The actual real Fredholm index of its fixed-end Cauchy–Riemann-symbol linearization therefore defines an integer $\mu(\phi)$ on every continuous Whitney class; it agrees with the actual index of each smooth fixed-end model, is additive under class concatenation, is zero on the constant class, and changes sign under reversal.

For an actual smooth finite-energy holomorphic strip with uniform generator ends, its actual Fredholm index equals this index of its continuously compactified Whitney class.

This proves a continuous-class index using genuine representatives and relative homotopies. It does not identify that integer with a domain Euler measure, corner multiplicities or a first-Chern pairing; no nonlinear moduli counts or their regularity are asserted.

Assume countable choice. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold with a smooth path $J_t$ of almost complex structures, and let $L_0,L_1$ be compact submanifolds totally real for $J_0,J_1$, respectively. Suppose their intersection is finite and transverse. At each intersection point choose a target chart in which $L_0=\mathbb R^m$, $L_1=i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t=i$ for every $t$. Retain those same charts and structures throughout.

A smooth fixed-end representative from $x$ to $y$ is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ with boundary on $L_0,L_1$, identically $x$ on one full negative tail and identically $y$ on one full positive tail. Its covariant Cauchy–Riemann linearization on fixed-end $H^1\to L^2$ spaces is Fredholm. Its real index is independent of the chosen smooth connection and of the representative under any smooth relative homotopy $H(h,s,t)$ with those boundary conditions, fixed endpoints, and one common pair of constant tails for all $h\in[0,1]$.

These indices add under concatenating two such representatives at their common endpoint, are zero for a constant representative, and change sign when $u(s,t)$ is replaced by $u(-s,t)$. Thus they define an integer index on smooth fixed-end representatives modulo the stated smooth relative homotopies, with concatenation and reversal laws. This result includes nonholomorphic representatives. It does not assume that a nonlinear moduli space exists or is regular.

A further relative smoothing and end-flattening argument is required to identify this smooth quotient with a Whitney-class set defined initially by arbitrary continuous disk maps and continuous relative homotopies. No such identification, domain Euler formula, or arbitrary-class representativity theorem is asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected Riemann surface, $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ with its standard complex structure, and $m\ge1$. For $a\in\Sigma$ put $E_a=\{a\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. This is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at repeated tuples. The universal incidence hypersurface $\mathcal E=\{(a,D):D\in E_a\}\subset\Sigma\times X$ carries a smooth complex divisor line bundle with its canonical section, whose zero set is $\mathcal E$ with multiplicity one.

For a smooth map $v:S\to X$, where $S$ is an oriented sphere or a closed disk, define $n_a(v)$ as the degree of the pullback point-divisor line bundle; for a disk use the canonical section to trivialize it on the boundary, and require $v(\partial S)\cap E_a=\varnothing$. The proof constructs this integer by elementary frame winding. It is defined even when a sphere lies wholly in $E_a$.

For a sphere, $n_a(v)$ is independent of $a$ on all of $\Sigma$. For a disk whose boundary tuples have all entries in a finite union of curves $\Gamma\subset\Sigma$, it is independent of $a$ on each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus\Gamma$. If $v^{-1}(E_a)$ is finite and the map is holomorphic on a neighborhood of every one of these points, then
$$n_a(v)=\sum_{z\in v^{-1}(E_a)}\operatorname{ord}_z(F_a\circ v)\ge0,$$
where $F_a$ is any local holomorphic defining function of the smooth hypersurface $E_a$. Each term is a positive integer. Thus the degree agrees with proper holomorphic intersection multiplicity, while divisor containment is handled by its degree definition and actual point movement rather than an unsupported proper-intersection assumption.

derivations.claim: Put $G=\pi_1(\Sigma,p)$. We first show that $G$ modulo the normal closure of all alpha and beta attaching loops is trivial. Use [F1] independently on the two disk systems; the boundary circles and the actual splitting are unchanged. Each handlebody is recovered from its boundary collar by attaching one two-handle along every compression circle and capping the resulting spherical boundary components by the actual cut balls. This is the reverse of the supplied product disk cuts: a disk collar is exactly $D^2\times[-1,1]$, its attaching annulus is $\partial D^2\times[-1,1]$, and after all such insertions the remaining pieces are the cut balls. By [F2], attaching each two-handle makes the boundary group map onto and kills precisely the normal closure of that circle; its collared intersection retracts to the attaching circle. Attaching a three-ball along its spherical collar changes no fundamental group, since that overlap is path connected and simply connected. Hence $\pi_1(U_\gamma)$ is $G$ modulo its own normal meridian subgroup, for either system. Applying [F2] to the two collared handlebodies in $S^3$ identifies their pushout with $G$ modulo both normal subgroups: a homomorphism out of this quotient is exactly a homomorphism out of $G$ killing both lists, the pushout universal property. The sphere result in [F2] makes that quotient trivial. Consequently the abelianization of $G$ is generated by the classes of the two attaching lists. All basepoint connectors in this finite argument are finite path choices. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

Suppose $m\ge2$ and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$. At the repeated basepoint $o=mp$, moving only its first coordinate defines a homomorphism $G\to\pi_1(X,o)$. Its image is abelian: represent two coordinate loops in two different slots of $\Sigma^m$, where the square map traversing their independent parameters is an explicit commutation homotopy. Their images are the same as moving the first slot because permutations have identical quotient image. Thus this homomorphism kills all commutators. We prove it is onto next, rather than assume the fundamental group of a symmetric product. [given, construct, algebra]

Choose any distinct tuple $q$ and a path $C:o\to q$ given by $m$ coordinate paths starting at $p$. A based loop at $q$ has a smooth representative, by finite chart subdivision and straight coordinate smoothing, fixed in a small ball about its basepoint. More explicitly approximate its finitely many coordinate segments uniformly inside their chart balls, smooth the finitely many joins by convolution in smaller overlaps, and use straight chart homotopies on these balls; the original based homotopy class is retained. In the smooth symmetric product the repeated-root locus has finitely many smooth multiplicity strata, each of real codimension at least two, as is seen from its disjoint coordinate-disk polynomial charts. Apply [F3] to the one-dimensional loop, fixing its small basepoint collar, with finitely many supported target-coordinate variations spanning the tangent fibers on its compact remaining image. A common small parameter makes it transverse to every stratum and hence disjoint from them, since the expected inverse-image dimension is negative. Off this locus the ordered quotient is an ordinary finite cover: disjoint root disks give the actual $m!$ local orderings. Subdivide the loop into finitely many such neighborhoods and transport one ordering; its coordinate paths end with a permutation of the starting tuple. In $C$ followed by this loop followed by $\bar C$, match the reversed paths in that permuted order. Each coordinate is now a closed path at $p$. The projected simultaneous product of these $m$ coordinate loops is exactly the original conjugated loop up to its harmless piecewise reparametrization. Changing their clocks one at a time in the product gives an explicit based homotopy to their sequential concatenation. Thus every loop at $o$ is a product of first-coordinate loop images, proving onto-ness. This uses no path lifting at a repeated tuple: the repeated basepoint occurs only on the explicitly chosen paths $C,\bar C$. [F3, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

For $m=1$ the balanced relation gives only $(h,k)=(0,2)$ or $(1,1)$. The surface is respectively a sphere or torus, so [F2] makes its fundamental group abelian; its identity map is the needed onto map from $G$. Thus for every $m>0$, $\pi_1(X)$ is abelian and is generated by images of the alpha and beta meridians, by step 1.1 and steps 1.2 and 2.1. Changing a coordinate basepoint or its connecting path only conjugates that meridian image, which makes no difference in this abelian group. At any generator $x$, moving its one point on $\alpha_i$ around that circle, holding the other points fixed, is a loop in its actual product torus. Its image is precisely the corresponding meridian image after basepoint transport. The same holds for beta. Therefore the images of $\pi_1(T_\alpha,x)$ and $\pi_1(T_\beta,x)$ together generate $\pi_1(X,x)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Given generators $x,y$, choose a path $a:x\to y$ in the alpha product torus and a path $b:y\to x$ in the beta product torus, both connected products of circles. Their concatenation is a based loop in $X$. By step 3.1 its inverse class is a product of an alpha-torus loop and a beta-torus loop, after transporting the beta loop from $x$ to $y$ along $a$ if necessary. Transport conjugacy is harmless because the ambient group is abelian. Insert these loops into $a$ and $b$ on their respective sides. The resulting loop is nullhomotopic in $X$ and still has its alpha arc from $x$ to $y$ and its beta arc back. An actual based nullhomotopy is exactly a disk extension of this circle map: collapse the final constant boundary of its homotopy cylinder. This is a continuous Whitney disk with the required two boundary arcs and endpoints. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Suppose the generator set is nonempty and fix $x_0$. For each $x$ use any realized class $u_x:x_0\to x$ from step 4.1 and define $$M(x)=-\mu(u_x)+2\sum_i n_{w_i}(u_x),\qquad A(x)=-\sum_i n_{z_i}(u_x)+\sum_i n_{w_i}(u_x).$$ Their values are independent of the chosen class by [F4]; hence these formulas define unique values without choosing class representatives globally. There are only finitely many generators in any event. For a class $u:x\to y$, [F5] concatenates $u_x$ with $u$ and adds its actual index and divisor degrees. Comparing with $u_y$ by [F4] gives exactly the two displayed grading differences. Any two functions with these differences differ by their common value at $x_0$, since every pair is connected. Thus each is unique up to one overall additive constant. [F4, F5, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

For an actual index-one class, put $a_i=n_{w_i}(u)$. The grading of its weighted output is $M(y)-2\sum a_i=M(x)-1$, while $A(y)-\sum a_i=A(x)-\sum n_{z_i}(u)$ by step 5.1. These are identities for every such class, including positive $z$ degrees, with no use of a count or differential-square assertion. For $m=0$ the target is a point and the constant model gives the final convention directly. Absolute grading shifts, invariant comparisons and nonemptiness were never used or inferred. [step 5.1, algebra] ∎

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 5.1 do not assert generator nonemptiness; gradings are constructed when a generator exists.
Step 6.1 handles the m0 point target.
Step 3.1 separately proves the only m1 balanced cases using sphere and torus groups.
Step 2.1 avoids all repeated-root strata only on the generic based loop; explicitly chosen conjugating paths may contain repeated tuples.
Step 4.1 constructs the two required torus arcs with precisely the given generators.
Steps 1.1,2.2 and5.1 use finite connectors and class-independent unique grading values, not arbitrary global representative selections.

boundaries.reason: No iff or holomorphic existence claim is asserted.
No absolute normalization or invariant comparison converse is asserted.
